item.title: After landing in US, Flavio Bolsonaro declares himself Brazil’s rightful leader
item.description: Bolsonaro lost Brazil's Oct 25 presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
After landing in US, Flavio Bolsonaro declares himself Brazil’s rightful leader Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro disembarking from a plane with his family after arriving in the US state of Florida on Oct 28. PHOTO: REUTERS

Published   Oct 29, 2026, 04:31 AM

Updated   Oct 29, 2026, 06:49 AM

Set as preferred source

Listen Summarise

Flavio Bolsonaro said he is Brazil’s “elected president” and claimed his Oct 25 defeat came from an “electoral coup d’etat” by Lula and the Supreme Court. He gave no evidence for fraud. International observers said the vote was fair. After refusing a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, Bolsonaro left Brazil for Miami with his family and thanked Trump and Milei for helping him leave.

AI generated

RIO DE JANEIRO - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who arrived in the United States on Oct 28, has declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil, alleging an electoral coup d’etat had been carried out by the country’s Supreme Court and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won the presidential election by over four million votes. Bolsonaro, who lost the Oct 25 presidential election and left Brazil for Miami, where he and his family received US visas. He thanked Argentine leader Javier Milei for helping him make the journey and US President Donald Trump, who granted him and his family entry visas, for welcoming him.

In an initial open letter posted on X, Bolsonaro declared himself “the elected president”. He then deleted that version, and updated with another letter in which he said he was the rightful “leader” of Brazil. “I want to say, not only to my 60 million voters but to the Brazilian people, that I am the leader and that the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organisation that has established a tyranny,” he said in the updated version. Lula’s victory has been recognised by Brazil’s federal electoral court, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party.

Brazil’s election took place in full compliance with legal and constitutional requirements, electoral authority chief Kassio Nunes Marques said in a statement, without referencing Bolsonaro’s letter. Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews about Bolsonaro’s comments, Trump declined to comment, reiterating earlier views on how it was “a very strange election” . Problem for Washington Bolsonaro’s comments pose a problem for Washington as it seeks to navigate a rift with Latin America’s largest country, home to the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earths.

Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaro family to help return them to power. Ahead of the Oct 25 election, Reuters reported on a US State Department campaign to restore the Bolsonaros to office. Washington has denied trying to interfere in Brazil’s domestic affairs. Trump has previously alleged Flavio’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution. Jair Bolsonaro travelled to the United States after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022. He eventually returned to Brazil but was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia. There was no immediate response from the State Department. Neither Lula’s office, the federal electoral court nor the Supreme Court immediately responded to requests for comment. Lula, who was himself jailed on corruption charges that were later overturned, said this week that it was “shameful” Bolsonaro had not stayed in Brazil to prove his innocence. No proof Bolsonaro left Brazil in secret after the Supreme Court issued the order, which relates to a money-laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing. Bolsonaro, who had been widely expected to win the Oct 25 election, did not provide evidence for the alleged electoral fraud. I Bolsonaro based his rejection of the result on the fact that a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice had extended voting by two hours on Oct 25 due to Lula campaign allegations of voter suppression in left-leaning north-eastern states. However, Bolsonaro’s campaign also sought an extension due to rains in conservative southern states. Bolsonaro lost to Lula by around 4.5 million votes. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis by Insper professor Pedro Burgos. Analysts say Bolsonaro’s request to annul the election result faces little chance of success. In his letter, Bolsonaro denied fleeing Brazil, saying he had left to protect himself and his family, and avoid being the victim of a witch hunt he accused Lula and the Brazilian Supreme Court of carrying out. “I want to make this clear: I did not flee Brazil,” he said. “I left Brazil, but I did not abandon the Brazilian people.” REUTERS

item.title: Lawsuit seeks to block Trump administration effort to find noncitizen voters
item.description: WILMINGTON, Delaware, Oct 28 - A Trump administration initiative to deploy hundreds of investigators to hunt for noncitizen voters is illegally intimidating naturalized US citizens and subjecting them to possible disenfranchisement, according to a lawsuit filed by civil rights groups that seeks to end the practice.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
Lawsuit seeks to block Trump administration effort to find noncitizen voters Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Published   Oct 29, 2026, 04:31 AM

Updated   Oct 29, 2026, 04:36 AM

Set as preferred source

Listen

WILMINGTON, Delaware, Oct 28 - A Trump administration initiative to deploy hundreds of investigators to hunt for noncitizen voters is illegally intimidating naturalized US citizens and subjecting them to possible disenfranchisement, according to a lawsuit filed by civil rights groups that seeks to end the practice. The lawsuit filed on Wednesday in California federal court by the American Civil Liberties Union and affiliates also alleges that the administration is demanding state election officials deny ballots to certain voters based on flawed eligibility data, potentially undermining confidence in next week's midterm elections. President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party is locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress, has repeatedly asserted that noncitizen voting is widespread in US elections, a claim that has been widely debunked.

Reuters reported on Wednesday that the administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas for records on tens of thousands of voters in at least a dozen states as part of the effort to uncover noncitizen voting. "The administration can't keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don't like," said Theresa Lee, an attorney with the ACLU's Voting Rights Project, in a statement. HOMELAND SECURITY AMONG DEFENDANTS

The lawsuit names as defendants the Department of Homeland Security and Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and US Citizenship and Immigration Services and Director Joseph Edlow. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In August, DHS launched the Unlawful Voter Initiative, which directed US Citizenship and Immigration Services personnel to generate lists of individuals to investigate for possibly voting without being a US citizen, as is legally required. In the months since, the Justice Department has brought more than 100 cases accusing individuals of noncitizen voting. It has also launched a legal effort to prevent California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters that the administration alleges are noncitizens.

The ACLU lawsuit said the initiative has led to thousands of fully naturalized American citizens being subjected to improper investigations, door-to-door interrogations and potential disenfranchisement. The groups alleged the initiative violates the Civil Rights Act and laws governing privacy and administrative procedures. The lawsuit seeks to vacate the Unlawful Voter Initiative and asks for the destruction of records that were created and maintained as part of the initiative. Last week, a federal judge in California placed limits on the Unlawful Voter Initiative in nine states, but the plaintiffs said those restrictions expire at the end of Election Day on November 3, allowing the initiative to be used in future federal elections. REUTERS
